analysis.one_liner: Makes the 2001 and 2003 income, capital gains, dividend, and estate tax cuts permanent.
analysis.headline: Introduced eleven days before the Congress ended, the bill drew no cosponsors and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would delete the expiration dates written into the 2001 and 2003 tax laws, keeping their reduced income tax rates, their low rates on capital gains and dividends, and their gradual repeal of the estate tax in place permanently. It was introduced on December 13, 2012, in the final days of the 112th Congress, referred to the Ways and Means Committee, and never taken up. It ended when the Congress ended on January 3, 2013.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households gain the most, because the largest pieces of the 2001 and 2003 laws were reduced rates on capital gains and dividends and the phase-out of the estate tax on large estates. Middle-income households also keep the lower rates the 2001 law set, though many of those were already on track to be extended.

how_it_helps.text: Deletes the sunset provisions of the Economic Growth and Tax Relief Reconciliation Act of 2001, making its reduced income tax rates and other provisions permanent rather than temporary.
Deletes the sunset of the 2003 law's reduced rates on capital gains and dividend income, keeping investment income taxed at those low rates permanently.

Because the 2001 law's sunset title also covered its gradual repeal of the estate tax, striking it would keep the estate tax repeal in place, sparing the largest estates from federal estate tax permanently.

analysis.who_pays: Federal revenue would fall permanently, adding to deficits that future taxpayers bear. The largest single benefits flow to households at the top of the income scale, whose income comes disproportionately from capital gains and dividends and, for a small number of very large estates, from escaping the estate tax.

drawbacks.text: Making the cuts permanent would permanently reduce federal revenue by hundreds of billions of dollars a year, adding to deficits rather than cutting them off after a temporary window.

The permanent pieces are tilted toward the top of the income distribution: low rates on capital gains and dividends apply mainly to households with investment income, and the 2001 law's estate tax repeal benefits only the largest estates.
Locking the rates in permanently removes the leverage they provided in budget negotiations, since the cuts were designed to expire precisely so they would have to be renewed by a future Congress.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: All taxpayers would keep lower rates, which is real benefit for working households, but the design of the bill concentrates its permanent value at the top: investment rates and estate tax repeal outlast everything else, and the revenue loss compounds year after year. An honest supporter of lower rates has to acknowledge that this bill's permanent feature is what costs the most and helps the fewest people.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with eleven days left in the Congress, referred to the Ways and Means Committee, and never moved again; when the Congress ended on January 3, 2013, the bill died with it.

narrative.text: Rep. Mo Brooks introduced the bill on December 13, 2012, eleven days before the 112th Congress ended.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the day it was introduced and received no further action of any kind.
No member joined as a cosponsor.
The bill never reached the House floor for a vote, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2013, killing it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained from this bill, because it did nothing beyond existing on paper for three weeks. The wealthy households and large estates it targeted were not locked into their rates through this vehicle; their rates remained in place only on a temporary basis under the existing law.

for.name: Rep. Mo Brooks
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to permanently extend the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts on December 13, 2012.

against.name: Rep. Dave Camp
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled committee action on the bill; it sat in committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no member cosponsored the bill, so the record shows no partisan lineup beyond one Republican sponsor.

industries.note: The bill would permanently lock in low tax rates on capital gains and dividend income, which flow overwhelmingly to households with large investment income, at the cost of permanent federal revenue loss borne by all taxpayers.
Striking the 2001 law's sunset would keep its estate tax repeal in place permanently, sparing the largest estates from federal estate tax, with the lost revenue shifting to other taxpayers.
